lines.raw: Chapter one. Conditional expectation, defined properly at last.
lines.spoken: Chapter one. Conditional expectation, defined properly at last.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> For integrable X, Kolmogorov's definition: its conditional expectation given the information G is a random variable that depends only on that information, and that has the same integral as X over every event in G. <bookmark mark='b'/> It exists by the Radon–Nikodym theorem: integrating X over the events of G defines a finite signed measure that vanishes wherever P does. Apply Radon–Nikodym to its positive and negative parts; and its density with respect to P restricted to G is the conditional expectation. <bookmark mark='c'/> It is unique up to a null set, and it is a random variable, not a number. <bookmark mark='d'/> When G is generated by a single event B, it takes two values, the elementary averages over B and over its complement when both events have positive probability. Values on null events are arbitrary versions.
lines.spoken: For integrable X, Kolmogorov's definition: its conditional expectation given the information G is a random variable that depends only on that information, and that has the same integral as X over every event in G. It exists by the Radon–Nikodym theorem: integrating X over the events of G defines a finite signed measure that vanishes wherever P does. Apply Radon–Nikodym to its positive and negative parts; and its density with respect to P restricted to G is the conditional expectation. It is unique up to a null set, and it is a random variable, not a number. When G is generated by a single event B, it takes two values, the elementary averages over B and over its complement when both events have positive probability. Values on null events are arbitrary versions.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> For square-integrable X there is a picture. The functions of the information G form a closed subspace of all square-integrable random variables, the plane. <bookmark mark='b'/> X is a vector above it, <bookmark mark='c'/> and its conditional expectation is the foot of the perpendicular: the orthogonal projection. <bookmark mark='d'/> Orthogonality says the error is orthogonal to every square-integrable function of the information, <bookmark mark='e'/> so the conditional expectation is the best prediction of X from G in mean square. Part twelve's least squares projects onto the smaller subspace of linear functions; the conditional expectation projects onto all of them.

X is a vector above it, and its conditional expectation is the foot of the perpendicular: the orthogonal projection. Orthogonality says the error is orthogonal to every square-integrable function of the information, so the conditional expectation is the best prediction of X from G in mean square. Part twelve's least squares projects onto the smaller subspace of linear functions; the conditional expectation projects onto all of them.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Four rules do almost all the work. The tower property: conditioning on more information and then on less is the same as conditioning on less. <bookmark mark='b'/> What is known can be taken out: a bounded function of the information behaves like a constant; more generally the product must be integrable. <bookmark mark='c'/> Information independent of X teaches nothing, and the conditional expectation is the plain mean. <bookmark mark='d'/> And Jensen's inequality holds conditionally when the relevant expectations exist. Every martingale calculation in this part is a few lines of these.
lines.spoken: Four rules do almost all the work. The tower property: conditioning on more information and then on less is the same as conditioning on less. What is known can be taken out: a bounded function of the information behaves like a constant; more generally the product must be integrable. Information independent of X teaches nothing, and the conditional expectation is the plain mean. And Jensen's inequality holds conditionally when the relevant expectations exist. Every martingale calculation in this part is a few lines of these.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The projection picture gives the law of total variance at once: the variance of X is the expected conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional expectation. <bookmark mark='b'/> It is Pythagoras: X minus its mean splits into two orthogonal pieces, the error of the projection and the projection's own deviation. <bookmark mark='c'/> So replacing an estimator by its conditional expectation given a statistic never increases the unconditional variance of the resulting random variable. To obtain a usable estimator independent of the unknown parameter, Rao–Blackwell conditions on a sufficient statistic. An individual realized conditional variance can exceed the unconditional variance. <bookmark mark='d'/> The same identity gave Rubin's rules in Part forty-one and the split of variance between and within groups in Part twenty-five.
lines.spoken: The projection picture gives the law of total variance at once: the variance of X is the expected conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional expectation. It is Pythagoras: X minus its mean splits into two orthogonal pieces, the error of the projection and the projection's own deviation. So replacing an estimator by its conditional expectation given a statistic never increases the unconditional variance of the resulting random variable. To obtain a usable estimator independent of the unknown parameter, Rao–Blackwell conditions on a sufficient statistic. An individual realized conditional variance can exceed the unconditional variance. The same identity gave Rubin's rules in Part forty-one and the split of variance between and within groups in Part twenty-five.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The definition conditions on sigma-algebras, not on events, for a reason. Pick a point uniformly on a sphere. Fix the same half-meridian, y equal to zero and x positive, in both panels. It has probability zero. <bookmark mark='b'/> Approach that half-meridian through a thin longitude wedge. The angle along it has limiting density cosine phi over two, piled up at the equator, because wedges are wider there. <bookmark mark='c'/> Approach the very same half-meridian through a thin geodesic band, absolute y small and x positive. The same angle now has uniform limiting density one over pi. <bookmark mark='d'/> The limiting set and angle are identical; the shrinking neighborhoods differ, so the answers differ. This is Borel's paradox: conditioning on an event of probability zero depends on the family of events it is embedded in, which is exactly what a sigma-algebra specifies.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> For whole distributions, one wants a regular conditional distribution: a probability kernel that gives the conditional law of X for each value of Y at once. <bookmark mark='b'/> It exists whenever X takes values in Euclidean space, or any complete separable metric space. <bookmark mark='c'/> The joint law then disintegrates into the law of Y and the kernel. <bookmark mark='d'/> Every posterior distribution in this course was one of these: Bayes's theorem for densities is a disintegration of the joint law of parameter and data, The kernel is unique only for almost every conditioning value under the law of Y. It may still be changed at a particular value of probability zero.
lines.spoken: For whole distributions, one wants a regular conditional distribution: a probability kernel that gives the conditional law of X for each value of Y at once. Every posterior distribution in this course was one of these: Bayes's theorem for densities is a disintegration of the joint law of parameter and data, The kernel is unique only for almost every conditioning value under the law of Y. It may still be changed at a particular value of probability zero.
